claims.text: Premelting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by surface-energy-driven elemental segregation.
Lower-melting-point components migrate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface enrichment by lower-melting-point components locally reduces the effective melting temperature.
A surface-initiated premelting layer propagates into the nanoparticle core.
The proposed particles are uniformly mixed solid solutions approximately 5–10 nm in diameter.
Slow annealing allows sufficient time for surface segregation.
Rapid quenching minimizes diffusion-driven segregation and preserves a comparatively homogeneous initial state.
Surface-energy minimization produces localized enrichment of lower-melting-point elements.
Localized surface enrichment creates a distinct core-shell configuration.
The segregated shell has a lower melting point than the core.
Selective diffusion can create a thin disordered or partially molten surface layer while the core remains ordered.
Slowly annealed nanoparticles will begin premelting at a lower temperature than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit a higher, more homogeneous melting point and less pronounced premelting.
The thickness or extent of the premolten layer will increase with temperature from 600 to 900 K.
The proposed mechanism should hold for nanoparticles below approximately 10 nm over the 600–900 K range where surface diffusion is significant.
Larger particles or particles heated in non-inert atmospheres may exhibit different behavior.
